passage: Tenzin, come and sit. Fifty years ago I had my interview for the teachers' college, and my knees were water. The night before, my brother Dorje asked me question after question until I could answer in my sleep. That morning, in the corridor, I remembered what my headmistress told me: stand tall, shoulders back, take one good breath. I did. It didn't make the nerves vanish, but it steadied my voice. Still, what really got me through was knowing my subject, because I had practised. A straight back helps, but you can't stand your way out of not knowing. That was me, Tenzin, your Nani Nirmala.

qa.q: What did Nirmala's brother do the night before her interview?
qa.a: Her brother Dorje asked her question after question.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling in the corridor, and what helped her?
qa.a: She was nervous, with knees like water, and standing tall with a good breath steadied her. She says the preparation mattered most.

qa.q: Which choice before the interview helped Nirmala most, and why?
qa.a: Practising with Dorje the night before helped most, because knowing her subject carried her; standing tall and breathing only steadied her voice.

qa.q: How might Dorje's help have felt for Nirmala?
qa.a: It probably made her feel supported and gave her real answers to rely on. His questions did more than a power pose could.

grounding: A teenager preparing for an interview stands straight and breathes to calm nerves, but relies on preparation.

passage: The rain had made Arnab twenty minutes late for the scholarship interview, and the waiting room was full. His aunt Kalyani had practised mock questions with him all week, but his heart was banging. He stood by the door, feet apart, and straightened his back. One slow breath in. A longer one out. He wasn't feeling brave, exactly, but steadier. When the panel called his name, he walked in and shook hands. He stumbled on the first question. Then the answers Kalyani had drilled came back, and he found his rhythm. Afterwards he told her, "The breathing helped. But the practice helped more."

qa.q: How late was Arnab because of the rain?
qa.a: He was twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling by the door, and what helped?
qa.a: His heart was banging, so he was anxious. Standing straight and taking slow breaths steadied him, and the drilled answers gave him confidence.

qa.q: What should Arnab remember for future interviews?
qa.a: Stand straight and breathe to calm nerves, but keep preparing with practice questions. Preparation carries the real weight.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt hearing his words afterwards?
qa.a: She probably felt glad that her mock questions helped and that he noticed. His thanks credits the practice.

grounding: A teenager before an interview stands straight and breathes, and credits preparation most.

passage:
In a small room at the Hyderabad community centre, Yusuf practised for his scholarship interview with Irawati Ma'am, who ran the centre's mentoring programme.
Before starting, he stood with his hands on his hips, chest out, legs wide, like a superhero he'd seen in a video. "It's supposed to make you feel powerful."
Irawati Ma'am smiled. "Standing straight and breathing slowly can help your nerves. But a pose won't answer the questions for you."
Yusuf dropped his arms. "So what will?"
"Practice. Let's go through the question about your goals again."
They did it three times. The third time, his voice didn't shake. He stood straight naturally, shoulders back, and took one slow breath before answering.
"See?" Ma'am said. "That's real confidence."

qa.q: What pose did Yusuf copy from a video?
qa.a: Hands on his hips, chest out, legs wide, like a superhero.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling before the practice?
qa.a: Yusuf felt nervous about the interview and hoped the pose would make him feel powerful.

qa.q: What did Irawati Ma'am suggest that built real confidence?
qa.a: She suggested practising the answers several times, while standing straight and breathing slowly, instead of relying on a pose.

qa.q: How might Irawati Ma'am see the superhero pose?
qa.a: She saw it as a fun but limited trick, knowing preparation matters more than posture alone.

grounding: A teenager preparing for an interview learns that standing straight and breathing help, but confidence comes from practice, not power poses.

passage:
"Manoj Bhaiya, I'm shaking. The speech is in ten minutes."
"Do the pose! Stand like this—" He put his fists on his hips and puffed out his chest.
Dilnaz laughed. "I'm not doing that in the corridor."
"It works. I saw it online."
"Maybe. But I've practised this speech twenty times. That's what'll work."
"Fine. At least stand straight. You're hunched like a question mark."
Dilnaz pulled her shoulders back. Took a slow breath. "Better?"
"Much better. You look ready."
"I feel a bit less shaky."
"Now go. And if you forget a line, just breathe and look at your card."
Dilnaz walked to the stage, straight-backed, and didn't need the card once.

qa.q: How many times had Dilnaz practised her speech?
qa.a: Twenty times.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling ten minutes before the speech?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt nervous and shaky about giving the speech.

qa.q: What helped Dilnaz more than the power pose?
qa.a: Her twenty practices, plus standing straight and taking a slow breath, helped calm her nerves.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Dilnaz's calm speech?
qa.a: Manoj would likely feel proud, and might realise her preparation mattered more than the pose he suggested.

grounding: Before a speech, a teenager finds that standing straight and breathing help nerves, but preparation matters more than a power pose.

passage:
Before my first inter-school debate in Class 10, I watched a video about power poses. I stood in the washroom with my arms raised in a V for two minutes, feeling like a champion.
But I hadn't prepared my rebuttals. When the other side made a point I didn't expect, I froze. The pose didn't help at all.
Zeenat, my teammate, whispered, "Breathe. Look at your notes." But I had almost no notes.
We lost that round.
Next time, I prepared for three days. Before speaking, I just stood straight, took one slow breath, and went up. My voice was steady.
The pose was fun, but practice was what worked.
- Lalit

qa.q: What shape did Lalit make with raised arms?
qa.a: A V.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling after freezing in the debate?
qa.a: Lalit felt embarrassed and disappointed, realising the pose hadn't replaced preparation.

qa.q: What did Lalit do differently the next time?
qa.a: Lalit prepared for three days and simply stood straight and breathed before speaking.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt during the round?
qa.a: Zeenat probably felt worried and frustrated, trying to help but knowing Lalit had few notes.

grounding: The narrator recalls relying on a power pose without preparation, and learning that practice builds real confidence.

passage:
Mentor's note, mock interviews for the science scholarship
Vijay came in with his shoulders curled and his eyes on the floor. Before he spoke, I asked him to stand, plant both feet, let his shoulders drop and take one slow breath. His voice was steadier after that, and his answer on the water-filter project was clear, because he knew every step he had built. Saurabh, next, had clearly watched a video about power poses: he stood with hands on hips, chest out, and held it before starting. He looked confident, but when I asked how his circuit worked, he lost his thread. Afterwards Saurabh laughed and said the pose "didn't work". I told them both the same thing: standing tall can settle nerves for a minute, but knowing your work is what carries an interview. Next step: Saurabh will walk me through his circuit on Thursday; Vijay will practise the breath at the door.

qa.q: Which project did Vijay explain clearly?
qa.a: The water-filter project.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he came in with curled shoulders?
qa.a: Vijay seemed nervous and unsure, eyes on the floor, until the breath and posture settled him.

qa.q: What does the mentor's plan show about confidence?
qa.a: It pairs a simple posture and breath to settle nerves with real preparation, like Saurabh walking through the circuit, because a pose can't replace knowing the work.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt when he lost his thread?
qa.a: Saurabh probably felt embarrassed, having expected the pose to carry him, though he laughed it off.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager using posture and a breath to calm interview nerves, and preparation, not a power pose, supplying real confidence.
